opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as the difference between the question and the tool. The lasting direction for me has always been the question: how do we get robots to actually be useful in the physical world — to handle contact, uncertainty, messy real environments, and to do it reliably enough that people can depend on them. That question was there before I worked on reinforcement learning, and I expect it'll still be there long after whatever method we're excited about today has been replaced.

Reinforcement learning is my current focus because right now it's one of the most promising tools for that question. Imitation learning and large pretrained models have gotten us surprisingly far — you can collect demonstrations, train a policy, and get behavior that looks quite good. But they tend to plateau. The policy is only as good as the data, and when it fails, it doesn't really know how to get better on its own. RL offers a way past that: letting the robot improve from its own experience, recover from its own mistakes, and push toward the level of robustness you'd need for real deployment. So for me RL isn't the identity, it's the thing that currently seems best positioned to close the gap between "a nice demo" and "a system that works."

The way I try to keep the two separate in my own head is to ask, every so often: if RL turned out not to be the answer, would I still care about the problem I'm working on? If yes, I'm probably on the right track. If the only reason the problem is interesting is because it's a showcase for the method, that's a warning sign. I've seen in robotics how quickly fashions change — from classical control, to model-based planning, to end-to-end learning, to foundation models — and the people whose work holds up are usually the ones who stayed anchored to the underlying problem rather than to a particular technique.

That said, I don't want to undersell the commitment. To make real progress with a tool, you have to go deep with it — understand where it breaks, build the infrastructure, run it on real hardware for months. So in practice I'm very invested in RL right now. But I hold it with the understanding that it serves the longer goal, not the other way around.

r001.rationale: Kay says RL “isn't the identity” and describes it as a current tool serving a longer-term research goal, rather than defining her research career.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of it as two layers that sit on top of each other.

The lasting layer is robotics as a question about embodiment. How does an agent with a body acquire general-purpose competence in the physical world? That question has been with me since graduate school, and I expect it to still be there in twenty years. It doesn't care which algorithm happens to be fashionable. In different decades the best available answer has been control theory, then imitation and demonstrations, then large pretrained models, and I've worked through several of those.

Reinforcement learning is the current layer. It's the tool I'm betting on right now because I think it addresses the specific bottleneck we've hit. We can now get robots to produce reasonable behavior from human data and foundation models, but that behavior plateaus at the level of the demonstrations. It doesn't improve from its own mistakes. RL is the one framework we have where the robot's own experience is the fuel, so it's the natural thing to focus on when the question is "how do we get past imitation."

So the distinction is really about time horizon and commitment. I'm committed to the robotics question regardless of outcome. I'm committed to RL only as long as it keeps being the best way to make progress on that question. If in three years it turns out that scaling data collection or some new model-based approach gets us further, I'll switch methods without much grief. What I won't switch is the problem.

I'd also say the two inform each other. Working on real robots keeps my RL honest, because sample efficiency, safety, and reset costs are not abstract concerns when a physical arm is involved. And the RL work keeps the robotics ambitious, because it forces me to think about systems that keep learning after deployment rather than ones that are frozen at ship time.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the lasting commitment is the robotics question, while RL is only the current method and may be replaced if another approach works better.

astra-6.text: I think of robotics as my long-term research direction, and reinforcement learning as one approach I’m exploring within it. The lasting question is how to make robots learn and act effectively in the physical world. My current focus is on how reinforcement learning can help us get there. The methods may change as we understand their strengths and limitations, but that underlying question is what connects the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics as the long-term research direction and reinforcement learning as one approach that may change, communicating that RL does not define the research career.

sol-6.1.text: I think of robotics as my long-term research direction, and reinforcement learning as one approach I’m currently exploring within it. The lasting question is how to build robots that can learn useful skills and adapt to the world around them. Reinforcement learning offers a way to study that through interaction and feedback, but the broader question doesn’t depend on a particular method. As the problems evolve, the tools I use may change while that underlying direction stays the same.

r001.rationale: The response frames reinforcement learning as one current approach within a broader, lasting robotics direction, and says the underlying direction persists as tools change.
